title: Biomolecules
description: Grade 11 Biology: chemical composition of living things, carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids, plus enzymes, their mechanism and factors affecting activity, and vitamins.

topics.title: Chemical Composition, Carbohydrates and Lipids
topics.concept:
All living organisms are made of the same kinds of chemical substances called biomolecules. By weight, the most abundant compound in living cells is water (70–90%), which acts as a solvent and a medium for reactions. The other biomolecules are carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids, plus minerals.

Substances are also classed as primary metabolites (directly involved in growth and metabolism — amino acids, sugars, etc.) and secondary metabolites (not directly essential, e.g. alkaloids, pigments, rubber, drugs). Small biomolecules (under 1000 Da) are micromolecules; large ones (polymers) are macromolecules (polysaccharides, proteins, nucleic acids).

Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen and are the chief source of energy. They are: monosaccharides (simple sugars — glucose, fructose), disaccharides (two units — sucrose, lactose, maltose) and polysaccharides (many units — starch and glycogen for storage, cellulose for structure in plant cell walls).

Lipids (fats and oils) are made of fatty acids and glycerol. They are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents. They store energy (more than carbohydrates per gram), form cell membranes (phospholipids), insulate the body and act as some hormones. A fat that is solid at room temperature is generally a saturated fat; a liquid (oil) is usually unsaturated.

examples.problem: Example 1: Which biomolecule is most abundant in a living cell, and what is its role?
examples.solution:
One compound dominates by weight.

  • Water is the most abundant (70–90%).
  • It acts as a solvent and medium for biochemical reactions.
examples.answer: Water — it is the most abundant molecule and serves as the solvent and medium for cell reactions.

examples.problem: Example 2: Classify glucose, sucrose and starch as mono-, di- or polysaccharides.
examples.solution:
Sort by the number of sugar units.

  • Glucose — monosaccharide.
  • Sucrose — disaccharide.
  • Starch — polysaccharide.
examples.answer: Glucose = monosaccharide, sucrose = disaccharide, starch = polysaccharide.

examples.problem: Example 3: Give two functions of lipids in living organisms.
examples.solution:
Lipids do several jobs.

  • They store energy (long-term).
  • They form cell membranes (phospholipids) and insulate the body.
examples.answer: Lipids store energy and form cell membranes (also insulate the body and act as some hormones).

recap:
• Water is the most abundant biomolecule (70–90%).
  • Primary vs secondary metabolites; large polymers = macromolecules.
  • Carbohydrates (C,H,O): monosaccharides (glucose), disaccharides (sucrose), polysaccharides (starch/storage, cellulose/structure).
  • Lipids = fatty acids + glycerol; energy store, membranes, insulation.

quiz.q: The most abundant molecule by weight in living cells is:
quiz.explanation: Water makes up 70-90% of a living cell.

topics.title: Proteins and Nucleic Acids
topics.concept:
Proteins are the most abundant biomolecules of the cell's dry mass and are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. There are 20 types of amino acids. Proteins do an enormous variety of jobs: structural (collagen, keratin), enzymatic (almost all enzymes are proteins), transport (haemoglobin carries oxygen), defence (antibodies), hormonal (insulin) and contractile (actin, myosin in muscle).

A protein has up to four levels of structure: primary (the sequence of amino acids), secondary (coiling/folding into helices or sheets), tertiary (the overall 3D shape) and quaternary (assembly of more than one polypeptide chain, e.g. haemoglobin). The shape determines the function; heat or extreme pH can denature a protein (unfold it) and destroy its function.

Nucleic acids are the genetic macromolecules, polymers of units called nucleotides. Each nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group. There are two kinds:

  • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) — the hereditary material; a double helix (Watson and Crick). Its sugar is deoxyribose; bases are A, T, G, C (A pairs with T, G with C).
  • RNA (ribonucleic acid) — usually single-stranded; involved in protein synthesis. Its sugar is ribose; uracil (U) replaces thymine (T).

examples.problem: Example 1: What are the building blocks of proteins, and what bond joins them?
examples.solution:
Proteins are polymers of small units.

  • Building blocks: amino acids (20 types).
  • They are joined by peptide bonds.
examples.answer: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, joined by peptide bonds.

examples.problem: Example 2: What does denaturation of a protein mean, and what causes it?
examples.solution:
Denaturation affects protein shape.

  • It is the loss of the protein's specific 3D shape (unfolding).
  • It is caused by heat or extreme pH, and destroys the protein's function.
examples.answer: Denaturation is the loss of a protein's normal shape (by heat or extreme pH), which destroys its function.

examples.problem: Example 3: State two differences between DNA and RNA.
examples.solution:
Compare sugar and bases.

  • DNA has deoxyribose sugar and the base thymine; it is double-stranded.
  • RNA has ribose sugar and uracil (instead of thymine); it is usually single-stranded.
examples.answer: DNA has deoxyribose, thymine and is double-stranded; RNA has ribose, uracil and is usually single-stranded.

recap:
• Proteins = polymers of amino acids (peptide bonds); functions: structural, enzymatic, transport, defence, hormonal, contractile.
  • Four structure levels (primary–quaternary); shape = function; heat/pH cause denaturation.
  • Nucleic acids = polymers of nucleotides (base + sugar + phosphate).
  • DNA (deoxyribose, A-T-G-C, double helix) vs RNA (ribose, uracil, single-stranded).

quiz.q: The building blocks (monomers) of proteins are:
quiz.explanation: Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.

quiz.q: In RNA, which base replaces the thymine found in DNA?
quiz.explanation: RNA uses uracil (U) in place of thymine (T).

topics.title: Enzymes and Vitamins
topics.concept:
Enzymes are biological catalysts — substances (almost all are proteins) that speed up the chemical reactions of the body without being used up. They are essential because, without them, metabolic reactions would be far too slow to support life. The substance on which an enzyme acts is the substrate, and the substance formed is the product.

The enzyme has a specific pocket called the active site into which only its particular substrate fits — this gives enzymes their high specificity. The lock-and-key model pictures the substrate (key) fitting the active site (lock). The enzyme lowers the activation energy needed for the reaction. An enzyme works in steps: the substrate binds to the active site forming an enzyme–substrate complex, the reaction occurs, and the product is released, freeing the enzyme to act again.

Enzyme activity is affected by several factors: temperature (each enzyme has an optimum; high heat denatures it), pH (each has an optimum pH, e.g. pepsin works in acid, trypsin in alkaline), substrate concentration (rate rises then levels off when all active sites are busy), and the presence of inhibitors.

Vitamins are organic substances needed in tiny amounts for normal functioning. They are fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) or water-soluble (B-complex and C). Each plays a special role and its deficiency causes a specific disease (e.g. vitamin C deficiency → scurvy; vitamin D deficiency → rickets). Many vitamins act as coenzymes that help enzymes work.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is an enzyme, and what is the active site?
examples.solution:
Enzymes are catalysts with a specific binding region.

  • An enzyme is a biological catalyst that speeds up reactions without being used up.
  • The active site is the specific pocket where the substrate binds.
examples.answer: An enzyme is a biological catalyst that speeds up reactions without being consumed; the active site is the pocket where the substrate binds.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name two factors that affect the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction.
examples.solution:
Several conditions influence enzymes.

  • Temperature (optimum, then denaturation).
  • pH (each enzyme has an optimum pH). (Also substrate concentration.)
examples.answer: Temperature and pH (also substrate concentration and inhibitors).

examples.problem: Example 3: Name a fat-soluble and a water-soluble vitamin and a deficiency disease of each.
examples.solution:
Vitamins are fat- or water-soluble.

  • Fat-soluble: vitamin D — deficiency causes rickets.
  • Water-soluble: vitamin C — deficiency causes scurvy.
examples.answer: Fat-soluble: vitamin D (deficiency → rickets); water-soluble: vitamin C (deficiency → scurvy).

recap:
• Enzymes = biological catalysts (mostly proteins) that speed reactions without being used up; they lower the activation energy.
  • High specificity via the active site (lock-and-key); form an enzyme–substrate complex.
  • Affected by temperature, pH, substrate concentration and inhibitors.
  • Vitamins: fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) and water-soluble (B, C); deficiencies cause specific diseases; many act as coenzymes.

quiz.q: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the:
quiz.explanation: Enzymes lower the activation energy needed for a reaction.

quiz.q: Vitamins A, D, E and K are:
quiz.explanation: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble.

questions.q: The most abundant molecule by weight in a living cell is:
questions.explanation: Water makes up 70-90% of the cell.

questions.q: Substances like alkaloids and pigments, not directly essential for growth, are:
questions.explanation: Secondary metabolites (alkaloids, pigments) are not directly essential.

questions.q: The chief source of energy in the body is:
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are the main energy source.

questions.q: Cellulose, found in plant cell walls, is a:
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide.

questions.q: Lipids are made of glycerol and:
questions.explanation: Lipids are made of fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.q: The building blocks of proteins are:
questions.explanation: Proteins are polymers of amino acids.

questions.q: The bond that joins amino acids in a protein is the:
questions.explanation: Amino acids join by peptide bonds.

questions.q: Loss of a protein's normal shape due to heat or pH is called:
questions.explanation: Denaturation is the loss of a protein's specific shape and function.

questions.q: The monomers of nucleic acids are:
questions.explanation: Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides.

questions.q: In DNA, adenine (A) pairs with:
questions.explanation: A pairs with T (and G with C) in DNA.

questions.q: RNA differs from DNA in having the base:
questions.explanation: RNA has uracil in place of thymine.

questions.q: Biological catalysts that speed up reactions are:
questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts.

questions.q: The specific pocket of an enzyme where the substrate binds is the:
questions.explanation: The substrate binds at the enzyme's active site.

questions.q: Which factor does NOT directly affect enzyme activity?
questions.explanation: Temperature, pH and substrate concentration affect enzymes; container colour does not.

questions.q: Deficiency of vitamin C causes:
questions.explanation: Lack of vitamin C causes scurvy.

questions.q: Per gram, fats store more energy than carbohydrates, which is why the body uses fat for:
questions.explanation: Energy-dense fats are ideal for compact, long-term energy storage; carbohydrates give quick energy.

questions.q: An enzyme acts only on one specific substrate because:
options: Only that substrate fits its active site (lock-and-key)
questions.explanation: Specificity comes from the unique shape of the active site, which fits only its substrate.

questions.q: Boiling a solution of the enzyme amylase stops it digesting starch because heat:
options: Denatures the enzyme, destroying its active site
questions.explanation: High heat denatures the protein enzyme, so the active site no longer works.

questions.q: Pepsin works best in the stomach and trypsin in the intestine. This shows that enzymes have an optimum:
questions.explanation: Pepsin's optimum is acidic, trypsin's is alkaline — each enzyme has an optimum pH.

questions.q: Increasing substrate concentration speeds up an enzyme reaction up to a point, after which the rate levels off because:
options: All the enzyme active sites become occupied (saturated)
questions.explanation: Once every active site is busy, adding more substrate cannot increase the rate further.

questions.q: Many B-complex vitamins are needed in tiny amounts because they act as:
questions.explanation: Several vitamins serve as coenzymes, assisting enzyme-catalysed reactions, so only small amounts are needed.
